doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Union ban and odd jobs in Toronto, ending with a kind boss in a shirt shop
summary: Told to wait a year for a union card, he worked as elevator operator, clerk and shop salesman, and his boss let him play a matinee.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: So you liked Canada and you found work?

I went back, and after I finished my 18 months in Bermuda I went back home to England and I told my parents that I wanted to emigrate. I couldn’t see any future in England. I was sitting in this old radio gig, in this old railway carriage, and it was so depressing and everything. And I thought eh, I think I’ll give it a try. And so I went back. The thing didn’t work out with the girl. And when I went to join the union, it was an ex-Brit there. And he said, “Oh, where did you come from?” I said, “Well I came from England but I was in Bermuda working.” “You shouldn’t have been working there.” I said, “What do you mean I shouldn’t?” He said, “That’s American Federation of Musicians territory.” I said, “Well I accepted the gig in England on Waldorf Street,” I said, “I knew nothing about that, I just wanted to work.” He said, “Go away and don’t come back for a year, and don’t play a note.”

So I wanted to join the union and I knew I couldn’t get started. In those days if they caught you sitting in they’d fine you a whole bunch of money. It was terrible. They got rid of that particular group of union people. It was almost like the Spanish Inquisition, you know. Anyway, I got a job as an elevator operator in the biggest hotel, but I got elevator sick because the damn thing would go up and down. I’d get people caught in the © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

doors. Then I was working selling sporting goods and tobacco in a big department store. Then I went from there to a room clerk at the King Edward Hotel, which is a fancy hotel, and I stuck that out, but it was nights — 11 at night ‘til 8 in the morning. I did it for about six months. But I was determined. I never even thought about going on welfare you know, like a lot of people do today, because it was a disgrace in England to go on the dole, you wouldn’t do it. And then I wound up working in a shirt shop, and the guy that owned it happened to be a runner for Al Capone.
Yeah. Milt Hinton used to do that.

He was a driver, or an assistant. Anyway, I got into this nice clothing store and about the time, after about three or four weeks, I got my union card, and I got a gig in a bar. And I had to do a Saturday matinee you see? Oh, how the hell am I going to get away to do this matinee on a Saturday with a clothing store. So I told my manager. He said, “Peter,” he said, “take your lunch from 3 to 4 and if Harry asks where you are I’ll say you’ve gone off on an errand from 4 to 5” you see. The place wasn’t very far away, I could whip into it. So I pulled this off for about three weeks, and Harry was — you know like George Raft, remember George Raft?

And he looked like a gangster, dressed so smart and he’d stand there. And if he was doing this much he was really animated you know. So I came in this Saturday and he said, “Where do you go on a Saturday afternoon?” I said, “Mr. Field, I’ve got to tell you, I’m a musician and I do this matinee. I’ve really waited a year for the union card and I would appreciate it, I’m awfully sorry, anything I can do? Some extra hours?” “What time do you finish at night?” I said, “One in the morning.” Oh yeah, and you have to drive up to North Toronto, that’s two o’clock by the time you get to bed, and you’ve got to get up at seven to get here.” And then he said, “Why don’t you come in executive hours? Come in at ten in the morning and take Saturday afternoons off?” I thought then he is going to say yeah, and don’t do it on my time, you’re fired. And then he said to me, “And if it doesn’t work out, Peter, you’ve still got a job here.”
